summary: A consultant-level tour of liberation from ventilation. Short pressure-support breathing trials (Subira 2019) increase successful extubation without raising reintubation, though TIP-EX (2022) found no ventilator-free-day benefit in high-risk patients; 2024 meta-analyses favour pressure augmentation. After extubation, high-flow beats standard oxygen in low-risk patients, and in high-risk patients high-flow alternating with NIV (HIGH-WEAN) or humidified NIV in very high risk reduces reintubation; ATS/CHEST 2017 and ERS 2022 favour NIV for high risk. Prophylactic methylprednisolone works mainly in patients who fail a cuff leak test, a test with high specificity but modest sensitivity. TracMan showed no mortality benefit from tracheostomy within four days and showed how poorly clinicians predict prolonged ventilation; Cochrane 2015 hinted at benefit, and SETPOINT2 was neutral in stroke. Percutaneous and surgical techniques have similar serious complication rates, with fewer wound infections after percutaneous. UK safety work (NAP4, the NTSP 2020 guidance and the 20-hospital improvement programme) centres on care after insertion. Prolonged weaning (WIND) carries high mortality; diaphragm atrophy predicts prolonged ventilation; and RESCUE-3 phrenic stimulation (2026) is promising but stopped early, with more serious adverse events.
takeaways: A short pressure support SBT is fine for most patients and doesn't increase reintubation.
High-risk patients go on to high-flow alternating with NIV after extubation; low-risk patients get high-flow.
Do a cuff leak test in high-risk patients; if it fails, give steroids at least four hours ahead, ideally twelve.
In TracMan, early tracheostomy didn't save lives: decide case by case and remember how badly we predict who will need one.
Use NTSP bedhead signs, emergency algorithms and capnography for every tracheostomy, every time.
